entities.summary:
Charles Somerset, 1st Earl of Worcester (1502-1526), was an English nobleman and politician, illegitimate son of Henry Beaufort, 3rd Duke of Somerset, by his mistress Joan Hill.

Born into a lower noble family, Somerset's life was marked by his efforts to assert his family's claim to the dukedom of Somerset and secure a more prominent position in the royal court. He was a skilled diplomat and strategist, using his connections to further the interests of his family and the English monarchy.

Somerset's most notable achievement was his role in the negotiations leading to the Treaty of London in 1520, which ended a long-standing conflict with the Holy Roman Empire. This treaty secured significant trade agreements and established a crucial alliance between England and the Holy Roman Empire, cementing Somerset's reputation as a skilled diplomat.

Despite his successes, Somerset's life was cut short when he died on March 15, 1526, at the age of 24. His death marked the end of a promising career, but his legacy lived on through his family's continued involvement in English politics.

Somerset's story serves as a reminder of the complex web of alliances and rivalries that defined the medieval period, and the critical role that individuals like Somerset played in shaping the course of European history.

In the words of the 16th-century historian Polydore Vergil, 'Somerset, Earl of Worcester, was a man of great virtue and excellent judgment, who, in his time, did much to promote the interests of his lord and country.'
